utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. We will have the accused brought in, please. All right. Shall we have the witness brought in? We're a little late this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall try to hurry up. I should like to say good morning to Mr. Ramic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You are here. Yes, well, let us try now to make up for the time we lost. Mr. Greaves, do you think you can help us with that? I should like to say good morning to the interpreters and everybody else, to the counsel for the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused, and we shall begin. Mr. Greaves, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, we were talking yesterday, and I would like you to have again the list that you prepared in front of you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, can I ask you to look, please, at Number 13, Suljevic Hamdija. Again, in relation to him, can you say from whom it was that you heard that he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, what list? I'm not really -- oh, yes, it was the list which was submitted to us by the Prosecution. It is the original list, the Exhibit Number 13, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I gave to the witness, Mr. President, Exhibit 59, Annex H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 13, Suljevic Hamdija. Can you tell us, please, Mr. Ramic, from whom it was that you heard he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say straightaway that Hamdija Suljevic was a personal friend of mine. I knew him very well. He was an elderly man, and he lived in a part of town called Gluhakovac. I heard that he had been killed from several persons, among others from his son, who today lives in the territory of Brcko that is under our control. There were witnesses who saw his dead body, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you given information as to when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 3rd or 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And any information as to who it was who killed him, whether by individual name or whether a group of people can be identified as his killers?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name? The name of the murderer I do not know, but I heard that he had been killed by a group of people who came from the direction of Bijeljina. And I heard that he was killed in a very harsh manner; that is to say that his throat had been slit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 15, please. We've discussed Number 14. Number 15, Muhamed Jakubovic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was my personal friend too. He was an engineer who lived in Kolobara, and he worked in the Tesla factory in Brcko. So he was a man who was my age and who I was friends with from the days of our youth. And he was killed in Kolobara itself, on the same day when many other people from this settlement were killed. This was an entire series of people, and I heard that this man was killed by a man named Kosta Kostic, from Modrane, near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next page, please, Mr. Ramic, Number 18, Midhat Uzejrovic; I hope that's the correct pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Midhat Uzejrovic was also a personal friend of mine. He was one of the assistant directors of a factory called Bosna Plod. He was an economist, and he lived in the settlement of Kolobara too, near the health centre. I heard that he had also been killed by a group of persons who came from Bijeljina -- I don't know the names -- and he was killed on the 3rd or 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next few names we've had quite a lot of evidence about, so I won't go over those. Can I now take you, please, to Number 27, Muhamed Zelenjakovic, otherwise known as Lola. Again, if you can just give us -- without my going through the questions; you've got the format, Mr. Ramic. Can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muhamed Zelenjakovic was also a man I knew very well. He also lived in the part of Brcko called Kolobara. He was a man who worked in the hospital -- in the health centre, rather -- as a kind of janitor. I've known him from the days of our youth. He was almost 60 years old. And I heard that he had been killed, together with his son, also by people who were led by the name of the accused. The name of the accused is involved in this matter. Again, this is the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meho Sejdic, Number 28, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meho Sejdic; he is also from the Kolobara settlement, from a street which is called Osman Dzikic. He was an elderly man who worked, as far as I can remember, in the Izbor footwear factory. I knew him personally. He was my sister's neighbour, and he was killed during the first days; that is to say the 3rd, 4th, or 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any information as to by whom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the distinguished Trial Chamber allows me to explain, I would like to say that there were several persons from Kolobara who were killed on the same day. And I heard that orders were issued by the accused and that it was carried out by Kosta Kostic. So according to the information that I received, the killer of Meho Sejdic was this same man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next name, please, Mr. Ramic, Number 30, Ahmet Fatic. Same questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ahmet Fatic I think is the oldest man on this list. He was over 80 years old. I personally knew him very well. He loved fishing, and everyone knew that, and he did it from the days of his youth, and everybody in town knew about that, how fond of fishing he was. And I've known him from the days of my youth, because he lived in the neighbourhood where I was born. We heard about his death from a Serb who, at the request of his son -- that is to say, the son of Ahmet Fatic lives in a place called Srebrenik. He went to bury him, and he found him killed at his doorstep, and that's where he buried him. We heard that he had also been killed by the mentioned Kosta Kostic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 31, please, the father of Dr. Fatic. The same questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty-one is the father of Dr. Fatic. I cannot remember his first name with certainty. I think it was Omer. He was an elderly man. He was 75 to 80 years old. He was very sick; practically he was immobile. He stayed at home. We heard that he was killed in his home on that same day by the mentioned person. He also lived in the same neighbourhood, in the immediate vicinity of the aforementioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the mentioned person," is that Kosta Kostic again?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is Kosta Kostic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next page, please, Mr. Ramic, if you'd be so kind. Osman Suljic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Osman Suljic was a student. He studied mechanical engineering in Sarajevo, so he would have been a colleague of mine had he graduated. I knew him personally. I knew his parents. He was about 30 years old and he was killed at home as well, during this same assault; that is to say, with all the others that were killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 35, we've just got on the list a first name but not a second name. Having thought about it, can you add any more detail to the surname, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. At that moment when I was making the list, I could not remember the name, but later on I remembered the last name also. His last name is Huremovic, Selim Huremovic. He lived in another part of town. He lived near the bridge on the Brka River; that is to say, in the centre of town. I personally knew him very well. We worked together for a few years. I was a young engineer at the time; I had just started working in town. His wife was a Croat, an ethnic Croat, and according to the information I received, he was killed by a group that was led by the person who is accused here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Osman Vatic. Would this be right: He was, in fact, detained in Batkovic camp and remained there until much later in the year of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Osman Vatic. That's right. He was detained in the camp. Many eyewitnesses corroborated this. He was badly mistreated there. I must say that he was a lawyer by profession, and he was our Member of Parliament in the local parliament, but he was an invalid, a disabled person. He did not have a leg. He was detained together with his wife, who had been raped, according to the information we received, by the man accused here and his group, and she was forced to serve them in different ways. We received information that Vatic had suffered terribly and his psyche had changed terribly. The accused and the rest let him go home, but on that very same day or on the next day -- I'm not sure whether it was on the same day or the next day -- a team was sent to kill him at home, and that's what they did. They did that with another group of people who are not here on this list but who are on the big list where there are 100 names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mujo Borovac, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mujo Borovac. Mujo Borovac is a man who I also knew very well personally -- he was a technician in the local radio station -- until the very last day he went to work, and he was present when I spoke for that radio. He was taken away and his name's also mentioned as one of the persons who is missing. However, I found out from his family that they believe that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Enes Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Enes Jasarevic is also a man I knew very well. He was an economist by profession. He is also on the list of 100 names that I gave, and I gave a correction in relation to his name. He is also a man who was very well known in town. He was the son of my Sunday school teacher, a very well-known person in town. We heard that he was killed by a group led by the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final name, Izudin Brodlic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izudin Brodlic is an elderly man. He was about 70 years old; 70, 75. He was a neighbour of mine. He was a neighbour of my parents, actually, and a man whom I knew pretty well. He had two daughters and one son. His daughter was married to a friend of mine, Dr. Kanlic. He was also one of the prominent citizens in town. He was not killed during the first days. He was killed, according to the information we have, about two months later; that is to say, in the month of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now have a look, please, at Exhibit 59I? If I could go, please, to number 14, Sadik Ljaljic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sadik Ljaljic is a man whom I knew well. He was elderly man, about 60 years old. He worked on central heating. He worked in the municipality. He worked for me. Before I became mayor, I knew him very well too. He was an elderly man who lived in the very centre of town. His house was right behind the police building, the SUP building. That's where he was killed. He was killed during the first days, I think on the 4th or 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next name, number 15, Ibro, son of Murat -- and I'm not going to even pronounce that one -- Vlahovljak?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your pronunciation is fine. Ibro Vlahovljak was an elderly man as well. I knew him very well. I mentioned Selim Huremovic on this last list. They worked in the same company where I worked as a mechanical engineer. He was a captain of a ship, and during the war he was a retiree. He lived in the same building where the mentioned Selim Huremovic Hurajmanovic was killed. So he was killed, together with him, by this same group of people during the first days of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 17, Mr. Ramic, Franjo Vugrincic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjo Vugrincic was a Croat who lived in a settlement which was almost purely Bosniak, which was called Meraji. He was a middle-aged person, and he worked as an electrician in the Interplet textile factory. He was killed during the first days of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next page, please, Safet Sahrimanovic, also known as Sarajka. Can you help us about him? Is this right: that he is someone who had a criminal past, had been engaged in criminal activities?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Safet Sahrimanovic, known as Sarajka, was well known in Brcko as a bohemian person. I could not say he was a criminal or anything like that, but his behaviour was a bit erratic. He behaved perhaps in a bit different way. There are such persons in other towns as well. I do not think that he could be considered a criminal. I know that he was killed by a group that was led by the accused. They forced him to run. They said, "You will be saved if you run," and, of course, they killed him on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people who were detained together with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 22, please, Muhamed Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muhamed Mujanovic is a man whom I do not know personally; however, I have received information that he was killed together with his son. His son is Meksud Mujanovic, number 19 on the same list. Both of them were killed on the same day, the 3rd of May. Muhamed Mujanovic that you're asking me about had a truck, and he was, therefore, involved in transportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed on the 3rd or 4th of May, during the first days, immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know by whom he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the names, but it concerns a group of people who are mentioned in connection with the accused, who committed a series of killings in a part of town called Mujkici. That's the area where he was killed. His dead body was seen, as well as that of his son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 25, please, Mr. Ramic, Bake, son of Atif, Durmic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bake Durmic and his brother, number 27, Redzep Durmic, lived in the centre of town, in a settlement that we called Prnjavor. Its official name is Djermanovic though, and I mentioned that in my documents. He was killed during the first days of the war, on the 3rd or 4th of May, in the well-known camp of Partizan. Both of them were killed. Our information states that he was killed by -- I forgot his name now. That's a man who, together with the accused, participated in all the killings. I'm going to remember the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the name Ranko Cesic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Right. Ranko Cesic, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 26, please, Mr. Ramic, Sakib Becirovic, known as Kibe.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sakib Becirovic was a man in his 50s. He worked as a butcher in the Bimeks meat factory, and he was pretty well known in town. He was a very vivacious person, great fun. He was a patient of my late brother, Dr. Ibrahim Ramic, and inter alia, he was best man at his wedding. He was killed together with the above-mentioned in the Partizan camp, by Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 27, Redzep Durmic. Is he related to the former --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned him in connection with 25. They're two brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was going to check to see whether they were related. Thank you for pointing that out to me. Bottom of the page please, Miroslav Kljukijevic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Kljukijevic was well known in town by the nickname of Vogna. He was a man whom I knew personally. He was a ethnic Croat. He was a man whom I knew from the days of my early childhood. We went to school together and we were friends, very good friends. He lived in Kolobara; that is to say, in a settlement that was predominantly Bosniak. He was also killed during the first days of the war -- that is to say, the 3rd or 4th -- together with a group which, to the best of my knowledge, was connected to the accused who is present here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next page, please, Mr. Ramic. Number 39. I can't read the first name, but Rovcanin, a retired police officer.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Izo Rovcanin. Izo Rovacnin. That was a retired policeman. I do know that he died. I'm not sure how or where, whether he was killed or whether he lost his life due to the effects of the war. I know nothing in particular about that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just help you possibly about that. Did you hear that he had joined the Bosnia-Herzegovina armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly. Let me just tell you that I cannot say with any certainty where each and every citizen was. I knew that man personally -- Izo Rovcanin, that is to say -- and he really was a retired policeman. Quite possibly he was included in the defence. If he was and if he was killed, this probably took place in the first couple of days after the war started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, if I can just assist you, did you hear anything that he may have been killed whilst on active service, on or about the 8th of May, in Dizdarusa district?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that is correct. But as I say, I was not in a position to get information of that kind, but quite possibly that was how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next name, please,

utterances.speaker: MR. RAMIC
utterances.text: Admir Rizvanovic. Can you help us about this: Did you serve in a military capacity during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a citizen of a state that was called Yugoslavia, and like everybody else, I was duty-bound to do my military service, and I did this to best of my ability. So at the time, and when I was of an age to do military service, yes, I did. I served in what was called the Yugoslav People's Army. But that was 20 years before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about your military service to the JNA; I was asking about the period of the war. Did you serve in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or any other military unit during the course of the war that started in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday that my mandate as president of the municipality -- that is to say, mayor -- that in case of the outbreak of war, which is what we're talking about, I, by law, was at the head of a body called the war presidency. Of course I did not lead any military action, but I was at the head of a defence body in part of the territory that we called Free Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a unit, was there not, called 108 Battalion or 108 Brigade? Were you ever a member of that unit, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, precisely for the reason that I mentioned. That is to say, I was above this. I was a politician, so I led the authorities. That 108th Brigade that you mentioned was formed on the 17th of May, 1992, from under pressure of attack. So I did take part in its participation, the participation of the 108th Brigade, but I was not its member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admir Rizvanovic, from whom did you hear that he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from an eyewitness. Admir Rizvanovic was a very young man. He was just 17 years old. Of course, I didn't know him personally, but I did know some people close to him. I knew his brother, for example, who was a member of the 108th Brigade. In the course of those war days, he told me, on one occasion, his brother, this young Admir Rizvanovic, was killed during the first three or four days of the war. Days of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his brother's name?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His brother, I can't remember his name, but he had a very characteristic nickname, Talon, and I think that all the citizens know this person that went by the name of Talon. He is an invalid today and has one leg missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue to have dealings with or responsibility for 108 Brigade into March 1993, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, no. Let me tell you straightaway, after the establishment of the brigade, a system of military command was set up, and I, as a politician and representative of the municipality, had no direct influence on any activities whatsoever of a military nature. They had their own chain of command, that is to say, these military men from the top echelons of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I had no immediate influence on their activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware in any way that Admir Rizvanovic was in fact sill alive on the 11th of March, 1993, and indeed on that date received a commendation for his military prowess?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are in fact talking about somebody I mentioned a moment ago; that is to say, his brother, Talon. His brother received a commendation of this kind. And so, as I said, it was his brother who told me of the death of Admir Rizvanovic, and it was the brother who got this commendation for his military prowess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the brother also called Admir, or did he have a different first name?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can get that name for the Tribunal, but I can't remember the name exactly at this point. I think it was similar to Admir, like Amir or Asim; a similar name. But I couldn't actually tell you the exact name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please go to Number 52 now,

utterances.speaker: MR. RAMIC
utterances.text: Anis Preljevic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anis Preljevic is a young man. Here, as you can see, he lived in a settlement called Mujkici. And he was the son of somebody I knew very well, a woman working in the centre of town, at the pharmacy there. I knew her very well; that is to say, I knew his mother very well. Perhaps I saw him around, but I didn't actually know him personally. But what I do know is that he was killed together with his father, whose name was Seco, whose name is not on this list. As I say, both of them were killed, in the settlement called Mujkici, in the first days of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next page, please, Mr. Ramic, a group of names, 69, 70, 71, and 72. As far as that group of people are concerned, is your information that they were killed by Kosta Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I must add -- and I'd like to ask the Court's indulgence -- this is something I mentioned a moment ago. This is a group of people -- I'm talking about number 69, 70, 71. Safet Karamovic and Mirsad Karamovic are father and son. Began Hasanbasic was married to the sister of the above-mentioned Safet, so they are members of one and the same family. And they were released by the accused from Luka, but on the same day they were released they were sent -- and we have information that the accused issued an order to Kosta Kostic, who executed the aforementioned many killings in Kolobara, in the settlement Kolobara. And he killed 69, 70, 71, and 72 in the same place. They were seen dead in that same place, in a street called Osman Dzikic Street, in the Kolobara settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From people who were sent to collect the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they present, any of those people present when these orders were given, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of killings took place there, and they all took place on the same day. I cannot claim that they actually saw the killing of this group of individuals, but at that same time, they witnessed the killing of other people, people who had died that same afternoon and were killed by Kosta Kostic. Yes, they did see those killings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They may have seen the killings, but the question I asked was, were they present when the orders you claim were given were handed out?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aforementioned Kosta Kostic is a man from Bijeljina; that is to say, he is very well known to the accused. The accused was the commander of that group of people from Bijeljina who committed the killings, and witnesses claim that they saw him communicate with all those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, wasn't the commander of Kosta Kostic a man called Mauzer, not Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mauzer was the commander of the overall SDS area, the forces of the aggressor in the Brcko area. He was commander of all of them. But I should like to mention that the accused was in contact with the aforementioned Kosta Kostic. And how can you explain the killing on the same day that they were released from Luka, that same day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 78, please, on page 5, Mr. Ramic. Vlado Rebac. From whom did you hear that he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I do not have a lot of information with respect to that particular name, where and when he was killed, but I do know the man personally, very well. He went to school with me, so I know him very well. At one time he was the director of a catering enterprise in Brcko. He is a Croat by ethnicity. And I have no other information about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 89, Almir Tursic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 89 and 88 are two brothers, Almir and Aldin Tursic. They are young men who -- I didn't know them personally, but they were, in a way, members of the SDA party, the youth organisation of the SDA. Their mother was a salesperson. I knew her. She worked in a shop called Kluz in Brcko. And I have information that they both were killed in the first days of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Final page, Mr. Ramic: 97, 98, and 99.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a group of people killed, as far as I know, by the aforementioned Kosta Kostic, at the same time and on the same occasion. Muhamed Jakubovic, Pestalic -- it says "Pestalic," without his first name, and I should like to add that after seeing this list, I didn't understand who it was. But looking at his date of birth, I realise that it was a very old woman, as you can see, an extremely old woman, and her name is Lasli or Lasla Pestalic, and Mehmed Slomic. I knew him personally. He was about 60 years of age and he was -- his intellectual capacity was limited, but he was known in town as a very peaceful man, and everybody liked him. So all these three individuals were killed in the Kolobara settlement, according to information, by the same man, Kosta Kostic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it in fact right that the date of death of the lady, Pestalic, was on or about the 26th of June, 1992, and two men, Kosta Kostic and Dragica Todorvic, were involved in her murder?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, the killing in the Kolobara settlement at the beginning of May by the aforementioned Kosta Kostic includes this name too. And I'm not wrong -- I cannot be wrong there, because it was a woman, she was an invalid, she was immobile, and she was found dead, lying on her bed. She was bedridden.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would Your Honours give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the list, Mr. Ramic. I want now to turn to another subject, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much longer will you go on? I should like to remind you that the examination-in-chief lasted for around 35 minutes, that yesterday you took one hour, and today you've had 40 minutes. And I should like to hear, when do you think you will finish? I am really very sorry, but time is something that we should bear in mind. Even the Defence is under a certain constraint of time, even if not in the same manner. But could you please -- so now you have used two hours and five minutes, and could you please tell us, how much more will you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but Your Honours, remember, this is an important witness as far as the Defence is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I should like to remind you, in general terms, will you please try, will you please try to focus your cross-examination on the subject covered by the examination-in-chief, and you know I have already said a number of times why that is done. You are using two hours and a half for your cross-examination, and you do know that your cross-examination could be better synthesised at times. So will you please try to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't accept that, Your Honour. This is an important witness for the defendant, and this is not just a debating chamber where you turn a light on and counsel has to sit down. The defendant is facing a possible life sentence, and these are important matters that I wish to discuss with him. The list of people is a subject of part of the examination-in-chief, and I respectfully submit that I am perfectly entitled to go through those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will give you 20 minutes. It is 11.20, and you will have to finish by 20 to 12, and I will stop you then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now, Mr. Ramic, please, to an issue about which you asked yesterday, the importance of the town of Brcko. Would you accept that the town of Brcko is of strategic and tactical importance to both of the parties who've been involved in the Arbitration Commission; in other words, Republika Srpska and the Federation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this right: that to the Federation side, there are a number of features which make it important? First of all, if, as a result of the Arbitration Commission, control had passed to the Federation, that would effectively have cut in half Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think exactly along those lines, because I think that Brcko is in a specific position, and that through it, the Republika Srpska, both from the east and from the west, can maintain contacts in the proposed solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not talking about the solution at which the Commission has arrived at. The proposition I put to you was that if the Federation controlled and had as part of its territory the town and opstina of Brcko, territorially, that would cut in half one side of Republika Srpska from the other, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Court permits me, I will have to expound on that. I can't answer that question briefly. Can I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is very simple. You can answer the way you like, but we shall end the cross-examination at 20 to 12. So you may answer, and you may now expound the grand strategy of the war. That will only delay things, but it is really up to you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer would be as follows: A response to all these -- an answer to all these activities could be interpreted in that way, but I would like to say that we're going back to 1992, prior to the war, when Bosnia was a uniform state, and when there was no eastern and western part of some kind of Serbian republic, and there was no reason for anybody to ensure passage. It was accessible to one and all. From today's aspect, it could be taken in that way; that is to say, I could give a "yes" to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second importance of the town of Brcko is in its economic importance. Firstly, it has a river port which is the conduit for exports and imports of goods from Bosnia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Brcko has got a port, and from that aspect, it is important. But let me add that traffic via the port was not as important as was other means of communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to turn to that. Isn't it right also that it provides the centre of a road network which leads to, and is the conduit for, exports and imports to Eastern Europe?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say that. Brcko was a very well-trafficked area, but it was not the sole communications route. You could also take the Bosanski Brod route, or by Bosanski Samac to Zvornik, and to the west via Bihac. There were several crossings of that type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, do you want to contest the fact that Brcko was an important town? If it is not contested, I do not think it is really worth mentioning. Are you contesting that Brcko was an important town, an important crossroads?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then will you please move on to another question? Otherwise you will waste all your time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take part in the activities of the arbitration commission, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, not in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave no advice? Did you give evidence at all to the commission?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the proceedings of the commission? Did you take an interest in that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did take an interest, yes, but what I wanted to find out was what the results of the commission's work would be. I didn't go into detail, nor did I seek information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me about this, please: Amongst the items that you were aware of as being placed before the commission, were you aware that in the early stages of the proceedings, that the issue of whether or not there had been genocide in Brcko formed an important part of the submissions made on behalf of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons being advanced as to why Brcko should be handed over to the Federation side. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The side of the Federation, the Federation side, really did have that as one of its arguments, but if you want my opinion, I personally consider that that did not have any significant share in the decision-making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may not have had a share in the decision-making, but you confirm it was one of the reasons being advanced for Brcko to be handed over?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at all events, yes, but the strongest of all reasons, which we mustn't forget, was that the Brcko area was inhabited by a vast majority of the Bosniak population who experienced great suffering, and it was logical that this was a subject discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me about this. I didn't ask you yesterday. Did you remain a member of -- as opposed to taking part in the activities of -- a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have remained a member of the SDA, although I have fully frozen my political activities; that is to say, I no longer engage actively in politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you discussed with anybody in authority the evidence you were to give before this Tribunal? Not from the OTP, but from the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for the Prosecution of this august Tribunal. I did not talk to the representatives of the Bosniak authorities, if that is the question in this regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Ramic, I want to ask you this: You have asserted that you were not a military person within 108 Battalion, 108 Brigade. I suggest to you that that is not true, that, in fact, you were a member, an active military member holding officer rank in that institution.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would own up to you that I would be honoured had that been the case, and I wouldn't hide that, just as I did not hide my identity before this Tribunal, and but it would have been an honour for me had that been true, but it was not true, for logical reasons. I was president of the municipality, a politician who was above military structures, as mayor, and our organisation was such that politics were apart from the military structures, so no. But there is something else. Perhaps you have in mind my rank which I had at the time of the previous system, and I really did have the rank of officer in the Yugoslav People's Army. And as I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, I believe you already asked that question. He answered that he had a post in the municipality, that he participated in the establishment, but that he did not take part in logistic and military activities. That was already answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have one question for him. Are you aware that you are being sought for and proceedings exist in relation to war crimes allegedly committed by you as a member of that unit, and by -- and the location of those proceedings is in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to say, just as this trial is showing, ever since the outbreak of the war, we have collected a great deal of information committed against the Bosnian-Herzegovinian population about crimes committed, including the person accused here, and that that term --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a very simple question. It demands a yes or no answer. Were you aware of such proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asked a simple question, Mr. Ramic. Will you please answer the question "yes" or "no," "I don't know" or "I know," but please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about the proceedings. It was at a later stage that I heard that I had been accused of some war crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that before you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that you became aware of those proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the war, towards the end of the war, it could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date would you give to that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not really remember the date, but it could have been in 1994. We got a newspaper from Brcko, and it said that a list had been compiled saying that people who held the power in Brcko were being accused of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves, for concluding your cross-examination within the prescribed time. Mr. Nice, do you wish to ask additional questions, which is your right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but very quickly. Very quickly. Re-examined Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, just about the war crimes of which you've been accused. You say the people of Brcko were accused. Was it you or a number of people?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities -- I mean, in Brcko and -- I have to expound on this. Having heard that we had started with the investigation of war crimes, they simply countered and with a similar thing. So they simply covered all the people who held any responsible posts, either in politics or in the army, and they compiled a list of all those -- they covered -- they compiled a list of the names of all of those who held some responsible post, whether civilian or military, but they never really specified the crimes of which they were accusing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was my next question. Have you received any detail of the allegations made against you in any form, whether in the form of the detailed indictments published by this Tribunal or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Even that newspaper that I mentioned, that Serb newspaper from Brcko which carried that article, it did not mention anything. All it said was "war crimes," but they simply did not specify those war crimes. They did not specify the offences, nor times, nor site -- nor sites or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two very short questions on this topic. One, roughly how many people were named as the subject of war crimes allegations in this newspaper article; 5, 10, 15? How many?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a list with at least 30 names. It was the war presidency which I headed, then the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I need. That's all I need, 30 names. Since the publication in that newspaper, have any steps been taken, to your knowledge, to bring you or any of the other 30 names or thereabouts to trial?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think it is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next question: You've been asked several questions relating to Kostic and Kostic's killings, which you have connected to Jelisic. I want you just to give the best detail you can to the Judges of the source of your information and of its proximity or remoteness. First, was the information that Jelisic lay behind the Kostic killings something that you heard from one person or from more than one person? If more than one person, approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the things are beyond doubt. Kostic did kill, to begin with. Also, Kostic was linked to the accused --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. All right. All right. I will answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will just want an answer to that question at this stage. How --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will answer that. I will tell you. I heard from different people that Kostic was receiving orders from the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many different people, if you can help us?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be all that accurate, but I heard that from people who were in the town and eyewitnesses. Well, it could be about ten people or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next question is the proximity or distance of the information. Were these people who were talking to you about Jelisic and Kostic providing rumour or were any of them providing detailed information of the type: "I was there when the instruction was given" or "I was told by a person who was there when the instruction was given," something of that sort? How remote or proximate was the source of the information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people saw them talk. Of course, they could not overhear everything. There were also people who heard the accused, and that was one of the information I received, that the accused said roughly, "Well, never mind that. That one of mine finished off all those Balija," and information like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. One question about the strategic importance of the town of Brcko and its relation to the Republika Srpska. When was the Republika Srpska first declared or formed, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They proclaimed the Republika Srpska after the aggression. The first time I heard about the Republika Srpska was in late May 1992; that is, the name "Republika Srpska".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when it was suggested to you that Brcko divided the Republika Srpska, would you like to contrast that with the alternative proposition that it was the only way by which two separate parts could be joined; i.e., at the time of the aggression, was there anything to separate or was it still the case that there was something or some things that other people wished to join through Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question properly, but I shall do my best to answer it. Brcko was indeed an area in which the Muslims, the Bosniaks, constituted a overwhelming majority. If somebody wanted to set up a separate state on both sides of it, then he had to know that he had to go through Brcko. In order to secure that particular territory, he would have to eliminate the majority of that original population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the end of the aggression, how much of the original Bosniak population was left, in percentage terms?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned already that according to the information that we have, and according to our estimates and data in the town of Brcko, in the town, that is, and the aggressors' rule, there are only about 3.000 people left. We also estimate about 2.000 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 3.000 people represents what as a percentage of the overall remaining population? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three thousand would be -- would be some five, maybe six per cent in the municipality of Brcko. Or if you are referring to the town of Brcko, to the town of Brcko, then it would be eight per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then lastly, I've a few questions on the lists, in light of the details you've given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness take, please, first, Appendix H, the list of 39 names? I have, I think, five names to ask him short questions about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In each case, Mr. Ramic, I just want some -- may want some further details, if you can provide them. Number 9, you told us that -- killed with, I think, a number other people outside a cafe. What were the circumstances? How many other people? Where was the cafe?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 9 and number 10 are two brothers, Mustafa Medinic and Ado Medinic. They are young men of about 20 to 25. I did not really know them particularly well, but I knew their father. I heard it from a different source, yes, from different sources and from a number of witnesses, that they had been killed by a group headed by the accused. The latest information I received from their father, with whom I had talked on several occasions, and who is quite ready to confirm that -- be anywhere, including this Tribunal -- that on the 4th of May, the accused came from Brcko to Bijeljina, that he entered a butcher's -- and there are eyewitnesses to that, and it is corroborated, that there is a certificate, that their father has a piece of paper about that. So he came to the butcher's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My mistake for not making the question clear. I want you to tell us, according to the information you've told us about, where was the cafe, how many people were killed? That's all I want to know. Where was the cafe?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a cafe called Evropa, and it was in the municipal hall, about 50 metres from the municipal hall, about 150 metres from the police station. About 30 people, mostly young, between 20 and 25 years of age, were killed there, and those two were among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all killed at the same time, the 30 people, or at a different time, on the information you received?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all killed at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that cafe in relation to the very large hotel that's near to the police station, effectively opposite it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that aforementioned hotel, it is about 150 to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 15, please. Here I'm going to be asking you questions -- don't trouble yourself with why, but I'm going to be asking you questions that relate to other sources of information about these witnesses. You've told us about this witness and what he does. Does what he did -- start again. Did what he did, this man, involve making harnesses for horses or making goods out of leather?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This man knew how to do that, and that was what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 18. When was he killed, number 18?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 18, Midhat Uzejrovic, he was also killed on the 3rd or the 4th of May; that is, in the early days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Number 27.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muhamed Zelenjakovic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- him, just for clarification. Did he also have anything to do with a barbershop?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had two brothers, and they were -- and they had that barber's, and I went there. One of them was my barber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 37. Interplet is what as a business?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interplet is a large textile factory at the exit from Brcko towards Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that have anything to do with a television station, or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I need to know. Don't worry. Appendix I, please. That's the other list. If he can have that. I've got four names to ask about here only, and then I've concluded. Number 17 on the first page, the Croat, Franjo Vugrincic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the information coming to you, was there any explanation for why this particular Croat was killed? Alternatively, can you think of any reason, logical reason, for why this Croat should be killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjo Vugrincic, a Croat. Well, the reason for his murder, to my mind, is purely and simply ethnic. Because he lived amongst the Muslims, he was their friend, that is why they did not like him. There is no other reason. There is no other explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following page, number 18, the young man who was of bohemian behaviour and forced to run. When you say "forced to run," do you mean forced to run somewhere in the street in public, or forced to run from a prison? In a sentence, explain that just a little more.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the camp. He was detained with all the others and was subjected to ill-treatment, but they wanted to play a practical joke on him. As I said, "We'll let you go if you manage to cross over the fence and run away quickly," and of course, he failed to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following page, number 40. The commendation suggested as being in the name of Admir, and you said that was in his brother's name. If somebody were to show you a document -- I'm not in a position to do so, but if someone were to show you a document dealing with the name of Rizvanovic, would you be able to help us further? Anybody able to show you the commendation document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned his brother, Rizvanovic, who was an active-duty man in 108th Brigade and a very brave combatant, and yes, he was commended; that is also true. But I heard from different sources, and from him personally, that his 17-year-old brother was killed in the very early days in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Defence has a document that they wanted to put as the commendation, to check on the accuracy of this. I'd be grateful if they would provide it. I assume that they haven't got it; otherwise they would have put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 78, please, on the following page, I think, or two pages on. Number 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I just deal with that? We do have a document, but I didn't put it because I was fearful of being accused of intimidating the witness by making a positive assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I would prefer it, if it's -- if the document exists, I've got another observation to make in general about this in a minute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Greaves, but I must answer. The intimidation of the witness is something that the Judges decide about. I've never said that you were intimidating the witness, but it's a completely different matter to produce proof. I mean, if, when you ask a question which is merely an affirmation -- we're going back to a discussion that we had yesterday; I'm quite ready to go back to that. But I said that when you ask a question without producing something to corroborate that, then it may look as if you were trying to destabilise the witness. But we shall always be happy to see when you can produce a document. The Prosecution has asked you now, and now the Judges ask you, do you have a document to corroborate the question? It is not a matter of producing proofs; it is not a matter of intimidating witnesses. And on the basis of Article 98, I am asking you to produce the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that can be shown to the witness, and perhaps put on the ELMO, unless there is any reason for its not going on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a reason -- is there any need for confidentiality? I believe we can see the document to see what it is. Could we have it put on the ELMO, please, so that everybody can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ramic, first of all, we can see the name on the right-hand side. Do you know, just from looking at it, what the publication is you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a newspaper. It is a newspaper. It is a fragment from an article from a newspaper of the time. It is a daily, a daily newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The headline of the list of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The headline of the list of names, what does that say? Just help us. If you read it out, then the interpreters will read it for us. Just read the headline, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "I commend members of the 3rd Battalion of the Motorised Brigade of Brcko."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put it back on the ELMO so that we can follow what's going on? Does it say anything there about this person, number -- we can see number 4; "Admir" is the name given. Does it say anything about why Admir's name appears on this list? If you can just read out what is relevant, and then the interpreters will translate it for us.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are commended for military valour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does seeing this name in a list in these circumstances affect your opinion that it was the brother who was commended, and not Admir, listed as Number 40 in your list?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. It is a combatant whom I know, and I can't go wrong there. His nickname is Talon, and everybody knew it, throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the list here is wrong and that your evidence is correct? Or are you saying that your evidence may be incorrect on this topic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not wrong. I am referring to a man who was, for the duration of the war, in the free territory. He was the one who was commended, and his nickname is Talon. I am not wrong there. And I'm not referring to the man who is listed amongst the killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to the list, then, please. Appendix I, two more names only. Number 78, Vlado Rebac, Croat: Can you give a reason for why this Croat was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also a prominent citizen of the town of Brcko. He was one of the directors. We went to school together. When we were children, we were close friends; he was a friend. And he was probably someone who had to be eliminated for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, finally, on the last page, the old lady, number 98, Pestalic. From your evidence so far, it's not clear whether you're saying she was killed or whether she may have died of natural causes. Can you explain, please?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we received data about the persons who were killed from people who were forced to collect dead bodies. Her body was found in her bed. She had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How had she been killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firearms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could there be any reason you could think of why this woman, of that very great age, should be killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the central settlement of Kolobara; that is to say, the central settlement of the Bosniak population, where almost 95 per cent were Bosniak. These people were supposed to be eliminated; that is to say, to have the least number of Bosniaks possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my questions, Your Honour. The only other point is this: It's obvious from the detailed cross-examination by the Defence that they have quite a lot of information, or a lot of information about people who have been killed in this fighting, and it may be that they'll be disposed to adduce further details in the course of the Defence case. If there are further details they have -- and they've treated this witness very substantially as a library of information, rather than as somebody to attack. If they have further details that he can confirm or assist with, then obviously if they can provide us with the information now, we can check it, so as to agree it when it's forthcoming in the Defence case and to avoid, for example, recalling this witness or calling other witnesses to deal with matters that might be in dispute. It may be that Mr. Greaves has already provided, through cross-examination -- in the entirely appropriate way, as I accept -- all the detail he presently has. If there are other details, it might be thought sensible to exchange those details now, so that we can verify them before the witness leaves for Bosnia. Subject to that, I have nothing else to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that the witness should stay here? The Judges will also have some questions, but before that, we shall have a break. But does that mean you want the witness to be kept here, or do you intend to call him back again? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was simply saying that if, by chance, any part of the Defence case could be the subject of discussion or agreement now with the witness's assistance, then we could probably avoid even the possibility of his having to be the subject of a request to recall at a later stage. If, on the other hand, there's either no more information presently available from the Defence, for one reason or another, or if information comes by way of a surprise in the course of the Defence case, and if it's important information, I shall want to verify it, and it may be that I will turn to this witness, and I will then seek his assistance, at his inconvenience. So that's the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. All right, I think we shall now have a break of half an hour. The Judges may have some questions, so -- perhaps not so much a question, but of precision. Judge Riad will have some questions, but this is merely seeking some precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness Ramic. I should simply like to seize this opportunity to have the Exhibit P59, to ask you if the "H" which you added on various pages means that these persons were Croats. Is it that all persons where you have added an "H" are Croats or not? Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. All right. Now we shall have a break of 30 minutes, and the Prosecution and the Defence will try to reach an agreement. Thank you. The session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: C3. It is C3, court exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Riad, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have a few global questions to ask you, to make things a little bit clearer in our minds. I won't go into details, so don't answer me in details. Concerning the lists of killed people, the list of 39 and the other list, I realise that it covers a very wide range of occupations, that it goes from the president of the local executive to a truck driver. And then we see that it even concerns a woman, an old woman. And the age range is from 22 to 70, and I suppose the old woman must have been older than that, too. So what could be the common denominator between all these people killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I explained that this is obvious; that is to say that the link between all of this is religious and ethnic affiliation. I'm convinced that all of these people were killed because ethnically they belonged to the Bosniak people, or if they expressed certain sympathies -- that is to say, if they were oriented towards the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, just a second. So I would conclude from that that anybody of ethnic -- what you call Muslim -- was a target to be killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'll just continue asking about this old woman, Pestalic, who was killed, and I want just to understand what you said. You said she belonged to the central settlement of the Bosniak population, where 95 per cent were Bosniak Muslims and had to be eliminated. What is the meaning of that? Why did this part have to be eliminated completely?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for the town of Brcko to have the least percentage of the Bosniak Muslim population possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And, according to your knowledge, how much should have been eliminated? I mean, they wanted to reduce it to one fourth, one tenth, what? To keep nobody? Was there a plan?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive information. It was no secret. The SDS wanted to reduce the number of Bosniaks to below 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And how far did they succeed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that according to the information that we have and according to our estimates and records, that in town, at the moment of the aggression -- that is to say when the SDS military organisations took over power -- that there were about 3.000 Bosniaks. According to our information, about 2.000 people were either missing or killed. However, that does not mean that they could have eliminated everyone, because they were not within their reach -- the rest, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they eliminated also Croats, you said?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They wanted also to reduce the percentage of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: To how much?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that they wanted other ethnic groups, the non-Serb population, to account for a total of 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The whole thing? Not only the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All of them. Now, concerning the killings committed by, I think, Kostic, how far is Jelisic involved in these killings? In other words, Kostic was the executive power of Jelisic? Would he do what he asks him to do, and was he able to order him not to do? Or was he an independent agent, regardless of what Jelisic wants? What was Jelisic's authority in that case?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards that question, I cannot give you an accurate answer because I did not have insight into the actual relationships involved. However, the information that we received from the witnesses who overheard things, they say that Kostic killed people at the request of Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And just by the way, you mentioned that Jelisic went to tell the butcher to inform the family of -- I think the people who were killed, numbers 6 and 7 of the list. What was the purpose of this, informing them? Was it to spread fear or to express condolences? What was it? Why was he going on to advertise that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first, precisely. He wanted to sow fear among all the rest. And that is what the witnesses claim. With his full authority, he wanted to impose himself upon others and to say, "See how we resolve matters over here."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And that would lead, perhaps, to their running away? Is that the reason?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And this policy worked?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did. People would leave if they had the opportunity to do so. And that was the other thrust involved in their activities. They left certain people alive on purpose, because they got their property; they looted it or they bought it for peanuts, but they just wanted these people to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, a very strange question you yourself asked, and I want you to give me the answer. You said they would release people and then kill them the same day. What was the idea behind that? Who would be doing that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they wanted to reduce the number to less than 10 per cent. Therefore, they would leave some people alive. As for this group, they sent them from the camp to their homes, but at the same time they asked for them to be killed, through Kosta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you think this also could be linked to -- if it's Kosta, then it could be linked to Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that that is linked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Judge Rodrigues, you also have some questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Witness Ramic, the bomb explosion and the dead, you said amongst them there were no Serbs. Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explosion occurred early in the morning of the 30th of April. During the month of April, it was quite noticeable that citizens of Serb ethnicity were leaving town, all of them. When the explosion took place, it is only then that we actually realised what was going on. They knew that that would happen, so they left according to a plan; that is to say that they were aware of the danger involved. The group of people who came over the bridge was a group of people who were coming to see their families. We have received information that members of the Serb people had already been informed on all sides about what could follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question: Were those dead buried? Was there a funeral service for them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, there was no funeral. There was no official funeral. These dead were actually dismembered bodies. So this was an enormous mass of people that was there directly. They had come to the place where the vehicle with the dynamite was parked. So these were dismembered bodies, and we only managed to bury these parts of bodies that were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but where were they buried? Where were those remains buried?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I could not tell you that for sure. Please bear in mind that at that point, there was great commotion in town, and I, as mayor, could not have handled that at all. So an accurate answer would be: I do not know exactly where this happened. But what I do know for sure is that all the bodily remains were gathered and taken to be buried at the cemetery, of course, at the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The elections, who was the -- how did you vote in the elections; that is, something about the elections. The elections. Was it by secret ballot or not? How did you vote in the elections?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voting was by secret ballot, in accordance with the laws that were then in force. There were no problems with regard to the elections themselves. They were held in a peaceful and democratic way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: You said that you knew that some persons had voted for the SDA. How is it, then, that you knew that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could have been established after the elections, after the elections were completed. We received reports. That was no secret. That is to say, at every voting post. This was according to regional principles. It was well known how many citizens would come to vote there, what the ethnic composition was. We knew all of that, and then we got the outcome of the elections. So it was by pure mathematics that we could ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in relation to some persons, to some individuals, is it they who told you that they voted for the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such people too who did not conceal that. There were such people who did not conceal that, who said, "I had voted," and, "I shall vote." There were some people who did not conceal that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were some people who talked to you and said, "I voted for the SDA," but could it also be possible that some other people or those same people could have given you a whole range of information concerning people who were dead? Did they speak to you directly about those deaths?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand this question. Which people are you referring to and which death cases are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You compiled a list on the basis of information which some people gave you. You did not see with your own eyes anybody kill anyone. So you said that these people were dead because somebody had told you so. My question is: If we are talking about this same thing -- I mean, people confide in you.
